claim: Klp10A is a microtubule-depolymerizing kinesin of the kinesin-13 family.
source: Here we identify Klp10A, a microtubule-depolymerizing kinesin of the kinesin-13 family, as the first protein enriched in the stem cell centrosome in Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work on Klp10A's function (Rogers et al., 2004; Kobayashi et al., 2011; Inaba et al., 2015).

claim: Klp10A is the first protein enriched in the stem cell centrosome in Drosophila male germline stem cells.
source: Here we identify Klp10A, a microtubule-depolymerizing kinesin of the kinesin-13 family, as the first protein enriched in the stem cell centrosome in Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by the observation that Klp10A localizes to GSC centrosomes throughout the cell cycle but only to spermatogonia centrosomes during mitosis.

claim: Depletion of klp10A results in abnormal elongation of the mother centrosomes in GSCs.
source: Depletion of klp10A results in abnormal elongation of the mother centrosomes in GSCs, suggesting the existence of a stem cell-specific centrosome regulation program.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing elongated centrosomes in klp10A RNAi and klp10A mutant GSCs (Figure 2B,C).

claim: GSCs form asymmetric spindles when klp10A is depleted, wherein the elongated mother centrosome organizes considerably larger half spindle than the other.
source: Concomitant with mother centrosome elongation, GSCs form asymmetric spindle, wherein the elongated mother centrosome organizes considerably larger half spindle than the other.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing asymmetric spindle morphology in klp10A RNAi GSCs (Figure 3D).

claim: Asymmetric spindles in klp10A-depleted GSCs lead to asymmetric cell size, yielding a smaller differentiating daughter cell.
source: This leads to asymmetric cell size, yielding a smaller differentiating daughter cell.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing asymmetric daughter cell sizes following GSC division in klp10A RNAi (Figure 4B,C).

claim: klp10A functions to counteract undesirable asymmetries that may result as a by-product of achieving asymmetries essential for successful stem cell divisions.
source: We propose that klp10A functions to counteract undesirable asymmetries that may result as a by-product of achieving asymmetries essential for successful stem cell divisions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that loss of klp10A leads to excessive asymmetries (centrosome elongation, asymmetric spindles, asymmetric cell size) that result in GB death.

claim: Asymmetric cell division is a key process that balances stem cell self-renewal and differentiation by producing one stem cell and one differentiating cell.
source: Asymmetric cell division (ACD) is a key process that balances stem cell self-renewal and differentiation by producing one stem cell and one differentiating cell (Inaba and Yamashita, 2012; Morrison and Kimble, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior reviews on asymmetric cell division.

claim: The stereotypical inheritance of mother and daughter centrosomes during ACD has been observed in several stem cell systems.
source: The stereotypical inheritance of mother and daughter centrosomes during ACD has been observed in several stem cell systems (Conduit and Raff, 2010; Habib et al., 2013; Januschke et al., 2011, 2013; Rebollo et al., 2007; Rusan and Peifer, 2007; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies documenting asymmetric centrosome inheritance.

claim: Centrosomes play a fundamental role as spindle poles during mitosis to achieve faithful, equal segregation of sister chromatids.
source: As the major microtubule-organizing centers in the cell, the centrosomes have the ability to influence the segregation of many cellular components during cell division: most critically, the centrosomes play a fundamental role as spindle poles during mitosis to achieve faithful, equal segregation of sister chromatids (Meraldi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review on centrosome function and represents established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Aggresomes (damaged protein aggregates) are segregated asymmetrically to only one cell during cell division by being associated with a centrosome.
source: On the other hand, it is reported that aggresomes (damaged protein aggregates) are segregated asymmetrically to only one cells during cell division, by being associated with a centrosome (Rujano et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Proteins destined for degradation are targeted to the centrosomes and segregated asymmetrically during human embryonic stem cell divisions.
source: It is also reported that proteins destined for degradation are targeted to the centrosomes and segregated asymmetrically during human embryonic stem cell divisions (Fuentealba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Biased segregation of sister chromatids depends on the centrosomes in Drosophila male germline stem cells.
source: We have shown that biased segregation of sister chromatids (Yadlapalli and Yamashita, 2013) and asymmetric inheritance of the midbody ring (Salzmann et al., 2014) depend on the centrosomes in Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: Asymmetric inheritance of the midbody ring depends on the centrosomes in Drosophila male germline stem cells.
source: We have shown that biased segregation of sister chromatids (Yadlapalli and Yamashita, 2013) and asymmetric inheritance of the midbody ring (Salzmann et al., 2014) depend on the centrosomes in Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: Asymmetric centrosome inheritance was first described in Drosophila male GSCs, where the mother centrosome is consistently inherited by the stem cell while the daughter centrosome is inherited by the differentiating cell.
source: Asymmetric centrosome inheritance was first described in Drosophila male GSCs, where the mother centrosome is consistently inherited by the stem cell while the daughter centrosome is inherited by the differentiating cell (Yamashita et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: GSCs attach to the hub cells, which function as a major niche component.
source: GSCs attach to the hub cells, which function as a major niche component (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The mother centrosomes in the GSCs are positioned near the hub cells throughout the cell cycle.
source: The mother centrosomes in the GSCs are positioned near the hub cells throughout the cell cycle, whereas the daughter centrosomes migrate toward the distal side of the GSCs, and are inherited by the gonialblasts (GBs), the differentiating daughters of GSCs (Yamashita et al., 2003, 2007)(Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The daughter centrosomes migrate toward the distal side of the GSCs and are inherited by the gonialblasts (GBs), the differentiating daughters of GSCs.
source: The mother centrosomes in the GSCs are positioned near the hub cells throughout the cell cycle, whereas the daughter centrosomes migrate toward the distal side of the GSCs, and are inherited by the gonialblasts (GBs), the differentiating daughters of GSCs (Yamashita et al., 2003, 2007)(Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Klp10A localizes to the interphase centrosomes specifically in GSCs.
source: In the course of our previous study characterizing microtubule-based nanotubes (MT-nanotubes) (Inaba et al., 2015), we found that Klp10A localizes to the interphase centrosomes specifically in GSCs (Figure 1B, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Klp10A plays roles in regulation of primary cilia.
source: Klp10A is a member of the kinesin-13 family of microtubule-depolymerizing motors, playing roles in regulation of primary cilia (Kobayashi et al., 2011) and MT-nanotubes (Inaba et al., 2015) and in bipolar spindle formation (Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Klp10A plays roles in regulation of MT-nanotubes.
source: Klp10A is a member of the kinesin-13 family of microtubule-depolymerizing motors, playing roles in regulation of primary cilia (Kobayashi et al., 2011) and MT-nanotubes (Inaba et al., 2015) and in bipolar spindle formation (Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: Klp10A plays roles in bipolar spindle formation.
source: Klp10A is a member of the kinesin-13 family of microtubule-depolymerizing motors, playing roles in regulation of primary cilia (Kobayashi et al., 2011) and MT-nanotubes (Inaba et al., 2015) and in bipolar spindle formation (Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Klp10A localizes to the GSC centrosomes throughout the cell cycle.
source: Whereas Klp10A localizes to the GSC centrosomes throughout the cell cycle (Figure 1C, arrows), its localization to the centrosomes of spermatogonia (SGs), the differentiating progeny of GSCs, is limited to mitosis (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Klp10A localization to the centrosomes of spermatogonia (SGs), the differentiating progeny of GSCs, is limited to mitosis.
source: Whereas Klp10A localizes to the GSC centrosomes throughout the cell cycle (Figure 1C, arrows), its localization to the centrosomes of spermatogonia (SGs), the differentiating progeny of GSCs, is limited to mitosis (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: In both GSCs and SGs, Klp10A was observed on mitotic spindle poles, kinetochores and central spindle.
source: In both GSCs and SGs, Klp10A was observed on mitotic spindle poles, kinetochores (Figure 1E arrows and brackets) and central spindle (Figure 1B, arrows), a localization previously shown in cultured cells (Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 1B and 1E, and by citation to prior work.

claim: Klp10A is the first protein reported to date to be enriched on the stem cell centrosomes compared to the centrosomes of non-stem cells.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first protein reported to date to be enriched on the stem cell centrosomes compared to the centrosomes of non-stem cells.
evidence: This is stated explicitly by the authors based on their literature review.

claim: In wild-type GSCs, the mother and daughter centrosomes are equal in size with the mother centrosome located near the hub throughout the cell cycle.
source: In wild-type GSCs, the mother and daughter centrosomes are equal in size with the mother centrosome located near the hub throughout the cell cycle (Figure 2A) (Yamashita et al., 2003, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior work.

claim: In klp10ARNAi or klp10AThbA testes, the centrosomes proximal to the hub cells (presumably the mother centrosomes) in the GSCs elongated dramatically, reaching up to ~7 µm.
source: However, in klp10ARNAior klp10AThbA testes, the centrosomes proximal to the hub cells (presumably the mother centrosomes) in the GSCs elongated dramatically, reaching up to ~7 µm (average of 1.7 ± 1.1 µm, compared to an average of 0.56 ± 0.2 µm in control GSCs, N = 50 GSCs for each genotype), whereas the distal centrosomes (presumably the daughter centrosomes) in the GSCs were slightly shorter than the control centrosomes (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The distal centrosomes (presumably the daughter centrosomes) in klp10ARNAi GSCs were slightly shorter than the control centrosomes.
source: However, in klp10ARNAior klp10AThbA testes, the centrosomes proximal to the hub cells (presumably the mother centrosomes) in the GSCs elongated dramatically, reaching up to ~7 µm (average of 1.7 ± 1.1 µm, compared to an average of 0.56 ± 0.2 µm in control GSCs, N = 50 GSCs for each genotype), whereas the distal centrosomes (presumably the daughter centrosomes) in the GSCs were slightly shorter than the control centrosomes (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 46.6% of GSCs examined contained a visibly elongated centrosome in klp10ARNAi testes.
source: 46.6% of GSCs examined contained a visibly elongated centrosome (n = 277, Figure 2B,C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from microscopy analysis.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that the elongated structure was indeed an elongated centrosome, not a primary cilium, because it lacked the surrounding membrane found on primary cilia.
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that it was indeed an elongated centrosome, not a primary cilium, because it lacked the surrounding membrane found on primary cilia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,C').
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,C'.

claim: Elongated centrosomes were positive for three centrosomal markers examined along their entire length.
source: Elongated centrosomes were positive for three centrosomal markers examined along their entire length (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E), further confirming their identity as centrosomes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Centrosomes in SGs were not elongated in klp10ARNAi testes.
source: Centrosomes in SGs were not elongated (Figure 2C), suggesting that Klp10A's role in preventing centrosome elongation is unique to GSCs.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Klp10A's role in preventing centrosome elongation is unique to GSCs.
source: Centrosomes in SGs were not elongated (Figure 2C), suggesting that Klp10A's role in preventing centrosome elongation is unique to GSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that centrosomes in SGs do not elongate in klp10ARNAi testes, while GSC centrosomes do.

claim: The centrosomes in spermatocytes in klp10AThbA hypomorphic mutant were slightly elongated.
source: The centrosomes in spermatocytes in klp10AThbA hypomorphic mutant were slightly elongated, as reported previously (Delgehyr et al., 2012) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to prior work.

claim: In spermatocytes, both mother and daughter centrosomes showed the same extent of elongation in klp10AThbA mutant.
source: However, in spermatocytes, both mother and daughter centrosomes showed the same extent of elongation, in stark contrast to GSCs where only one centrosome is elongated.
evidence: This is inferred from the data comparing centrosome elongation patterns in GSCs versus spermatocytes.

claim: The centrosome elongation in klp10ARNAi was rescued by the introduction of an RNAi-insensitive UAS-GFP-klp10A transgene.
source: The centrosome elongation in klp10ARNAi was rescued by the introduction of an RNAi-insensitive UAS-GFP-klp10A transgene (nos-gal4>UAS-GFP-klp10A), excluding the possibility of an off-target effect (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result that excludes off-target effects.

claim: 73% of elongated centrosomes in klp10ARNAi GSCs were labeled by PACT-GFP.
source: We found that the elongated centrosomes were preferentially labeled by PACT-GFP (Figure 2D): 73% of elongated centrosomes in klp10ARNAi GSCs were labeled by PACT-GFP (n = 40/55), whereas the shorter centrosome was labeled by PACT-GFP in 0% of GSCs.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data using PACT-GFP as a mother centrosome marker.

claim: The shorter centrosome was labeled by PACT-GFP in 0% of klp10ARNAi GSCs.
source: We found that the elongated centrosomes were preferentially labeled by PACT-GFP (Figure 2D): 73% of elongated centrosomes in klp10ARNAi GSCs were labeled by PACT-GFP (n = 40/55), whereas the shorter centrosome was labeled by PACT-GFP in 0% of GSCs.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data using PACT-GFP as a mother centrosome marker.

claim: It is likely the mother centrosome that elongates upon loss of klp10A function.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that PACT is preferentially incorporated into the larger centrosome (irrespective of age) in klp10ARNAi GSCs, the above data indicate that it is likely the mother centrosome that elongates upon loss of klp10A function.
evidence: This is inferred from the PACT-GFP labeling data and the location of elongated centrosomes near the hub.

claim: After the induction of klp10ARNAi GSC clones, the centrosomes elongated gradually, reaching ~3–4 µm in length after eight days from the normal size of 0.56 ± 0.2 µm.
source: Interestingly, after the induction of klp10ARNAi GSC clones (hs-FLP; nos>stop>gal4; UAS-GFP, UAS-klp10ARNAi), the centrosomes elongated gradually, reaching ~3–4 µm in length after eight days from the normal size of 0.56 ± 0.2 µm, Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by time-course microscopy data shown in Figures 2E-G.

claim: The centrosome that stays in the GSC (i.e. the mother centrosomes) continuously and gradually elongates.
source: This result suggests that the centrosome that stays in the GSC (i.e. the mother centrosomes) continuously and gradually elongates.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course data showing gradual centrosome elongation in GSC clones.

claim: The GSC daughter centrosomes do not elongate even after they mature to become the mother centrosome once in differentiating germ cells (GBs/SGs).
source: In contrast, the GSC daughter centrosomes do not elongate even after they mature to become the mother centrosome once in differentiating germ cells (GBs/SGs).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SG centrosomes do not elongate in klp10ARNAi testes.

claim: The GSC mother centrosomes have an inherent tendency to elongate, which is counteracted by the function of Klp10A.
source: These results reveal that the GSC mother centrosomes have an inherent tendency to elongate, which is counteracted by the function of Klp10A.
evidence: This is inferred from the gradual elongation of mother centrosomes in klp10ARNAi GSCs and the lack of elongation in SGs.

claim: The GSC mother centrosomes need to be constantly anchored to the hub-GSC junction.
source: This might be because of the need of the GSC mother centrosomes to be constantly anchored to the hub-GSC junction (Yamashita et al., 2007), necessitating stronger microtubule nucleating activity throughout the cell cycle.
evidence: This is speculated based on prior work showing mother centrosome anchoring and the observed elongation phenotype.

claim: Overexpression of Klp10A did not result in any effect on the centrosome length.
source: Despite the striking effect of klp10A loss of function on centrosome length, overexpression of Klp10A did not result in any effect on the centrosome length (0.69 ± 0.26 µm in control GSCs, 0.71 ± 0.22 µm in klp10ARNAi GSCs (N = 67 GSCs for each genotype, p=0.70)).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data comparing control and Klp10A overexpression GSCs.

claim: In control testes, the mother centrosome organizes slightly more MTs than the daughter in early stages of the cell cycle.
source: In control testes, the mother centrosome organizes slightly more MTs than the daughter in early stages of the cell cycle (Yamashita et al., 2007), but the difference diminishes as GSCs reached late G2 phase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to prior work.

claim: The difference in MT organization between mother and daughter centrosomes diminishes as GSCs reached late G2 phase in control testes.
source: In control testes, the mother centrosome organizes slightly more MTs than the daughter in early stages of the cell cycle (Yamashita et al., 2007), but the difference diminishes as GSCs reached late G2 phase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Symmetric MTOCs led to symmetric morphology of the spindle formed during mitosis in control GSCs.
source: Such symmetric MTOCs led to symmetric morphology of the spindle formed during mitosis (Figure 3B, 100%, n = 20).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In klp10ARNAi GSCs, the two centrosomes showed dramatic asymmetry in MTOC activity.
source: In contrast, in klp10ARNAi GSCs, the two centrosomes showed dramatic asymmetry in MTOC activity.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing asymmetric microtubule organization in klp10ARNAi GSCs.

claim: In interphase klp10ARNAi GSCs, cytoplasmic microtubules emanating from the elongated centrosome were considerably more robust than those emanating from the shorter centrosome within the same cell.
source: In interphase, cytoplasmic microtubules emanating from the elongated centrosome were considerably more robust than those emanating from the shorter centrosome within the same cell (Figure 3C 64%, n = 28 G2 GSCs).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In mitosis, asymmetric MTOC activities between the long and short centrosomes resulted in asymmetric spindle morphology in klp10ARNAi GSCs.
source: In mitosis, asymmetric MTOC activities between the long and short centrosomes resulted in asymmetric spindle morphology, with the proximal spindle pole organizing considerably more spindle microtubules (Figure 3D, 54%, n = 20 mitotic GSCs).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In control metaphase cells, PH3-positive chromosome 4s were always observed at both spindle poles, and missegregation was never observed.
source: In control metaphase cells, PH3-positive chromosome 4 s were always observed at both spindle poles, and missegregation was never observed (0%, n = 14 mitotic GSCs, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In 90% of klp10ARNAi metaphase GSCs with asymmetric centrosome size, PH3 signal was observed only near the elongated centrosomes.
source: In contrast, in 90% of klp10ARNAi metaphase GSCs with asymmetric centrosome size, PH3 signal was observed only near the elongated centrosomes, whereas the shorter centrosomes were not associated with any PH3 signal (Figure 3G, n = 21 mitotic GSCs).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The frequency of chromosome 4 missegregation was considerably lower in klp10ARNAi metaphase GSCs when the two centrosomes appear to be similar in size.
source: Although it remains possible that missegregation of chromosome 4 is due to Klp10A's function on the kinetochore, the following observation favors the possibility that asymmetric spindle force is the major cause of chromosome 4 missegregation: we observed that the frequency of chromosome 4 missegregation was considerably lower in klp10ARNAi metaphase GSCs, when the two centrosomes appear to be similar in size (Figure 3F, 22%, n = 9 mitotic GSCs).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Chromosome 4 is essential only for development, not cell viability.
source: Chromosome 4 missegregation does not likely have immediate effects on GSC viability, because chromosome 4 is essential only for development, not cell viability (Gelbart, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on Drosophila chromosome 4.

claim: Abnormally elongated mother centrosomes in klp10ARNAi GSCs cause asymmetric force generation during GSC mitoses.
source: These results indicate that abnormally elongated mother centrosomes in klp10ARNAi GSCs cause asymmetric force generation during GSC mitoses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of asymmetric spindles and chromosome 4 missegregation in klp10ARNAi GSCs.

claim: SG spindles did not show asymmetry during mitosis in klp10ARNAi testes.
source: Consistent with the fact that we did not observe any centrosome elongation in klp10ARNAi SGs, SG spindles did not show asymmetry during mitosis (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with the lack of centrosome elongation in SGs.

claim: Klp10A is required to prevent abnormal asymmetry in MTOC activity during GSC division.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Klp10A is required to prevent abnormal asymmetry in MTOC activity during GSC division.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of asymmetric MTOC activity and spindle formation in klp10ARNAi GSCs.

claim: In control GSCs, GSCs established a spindle that is symmetric in shape and oriented toward the hub cells.
source: In control GSCs, GSCs established a spindle that is symmetric in shape (the two half spindles are equal in size) and oriented toward the hub cells, as reported previously (Figure 4A) (Yamashita et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and a citation to prior work.

claim: Mitosis in control GSCs resulted in a GSC and a GB of equal size.
source: Mitosis in control GSCs resulted in a GSC and a GB of equal size.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In klp10ARNAi GSCs, abnormally elongated mother centrosomes and the normal-sized daughter centrosomes organized an asymmetric spindle, with the proximal half being much larger than the distal half.
source: In contrast, in klp10ARNAi GSCs, abnormally elongated mother centrosomes and the normal-sized daughter centrosomes organized an asymmetric spindle, with the proximal half being much larger than the distal half (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Asymmetric spindles in klp10ARNAi GSCs persisted to the end of mitosis, resulting in asymmetric cell size with GSCs being significantly larger than their sister GBs.
source: Such asymmetry persisted to the end of mitosis, resulting in asymmetric cell size with GSCs being significantly larger than their sister GBs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a marked increase in the death of GBs in klp10ARNAi testis.
source: In contrast, in klp10ARNAi testis, there was a marked increase in the death of GBs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data using Lysotracker staining shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: GBs that are too small cannot maintain their viability and undergo cell death.
source: This might be because GBs that are too small cannot maintain their viability, and undergo cell death.
evidence: This is speculated based on the correlation between small GB size and increased GB death in klp10ARNAi testes.

claim: klp10ARNAi increases cell death and decreases cell size specifically in GBs (but not GSCs or SGs).
source: Although it is difficult to establish a causative relationship between small GB size and increased GB death, the fact that klp10ARNAi increases cell death and decreases cell size specifically in GBs (but not GSCs or SGs) (Figure 4C,F) implies such a relationship.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative data shown in Figures 4C and 4F.

claim: Time-lapse live observation captured an example of GB death following GSC division, where a small GB eventually lost nuclear integrity.
source: In support of this idea, time-lapse live observation captured an example of GB death following GSC division, where a small GB eventually lost nuclear integrity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no evidence for chromosome missegregation for major chromosomes (X, Y, second and third chromosomes) in klp10ARNAi GSCs.
source: By employing FISH method using chromosome specific probes, we found no evidence for chromosome missegregation for major chromosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is unlikely that chromosome missegregation is the cause of GB death in klp10ARNAi GSCs.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that the chromosome missegregation is the cause of GB death.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH data showing normal segregation of major chromosomes.

claim: Mitochondria segregated equally during GSC division in control/wild type.
source: Mitochondria segregated equally during GSC division in control/wild type, whereas more mitochondria were inherited by GB in klp10ARNAi testes (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: More mitochondria were inherited by GB in klp10ARNAi testes.
source: Mitochondria segregated equally during GSC division in control/wild type, whereas more mitochondria were inherited by GB in klp10ARNAi testes (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: It is unlikely that missegregation of mitochondria explains the higher frequency of GB death in klp10ARNAi testes.
source: Because GBs inherited more mitochondria than GSCs, it is unlikely that missegregation of mitochondria explains the higher frequency of GB death.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GBs inherit more mitochondria, which would not be expected to cause cell death.

claim: Golgi was observed to be inherited predominantly by GBs during control/wild type GSC divisions.
source: Golgi was observed to be inherited predominantly by GBs during control/wild type GSC divisions, whereas GSCs inherited more Golgi upon knockdown of klp10A (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: GSCs inherited more Golgi upon knockdown of klp10A.
source: Golgi was observed to be inherited predominantly by GBs during control/wild type GSC divisions, whereas GSCs inherited more Golgi upon knockdown of klp10A (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Asymmetric spindle in klp10ARNAi GSCs results in altered patterns of organelle segregation, which might collectively compromise the viability of GBs.
source: In summary, although it remains unclear whether the perturbed segregation patterns of any single organelle can explain the frequent GB death, these data suggest that asymmetric spindle in klp10ARNAi GSCs results in altered patterns of organelle segregation, which might collectively compromise the viability of GBs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed alterations in organelle segregation patterns.

claim: A cell size checkpoint may be in operation, possibly eliminating cells that are too small.
source: Alternatively, a cell size checkpoint may be in operation, possibly eliminating cells that are too small (Kellogg, 2003).
evidence: This is speculated as an alternative explanation for GB death, supported by a citation to prior work on cell size checkpoints.

claim: A cell competition mechanism might lead to elimination of unfit cells.
source: It is also possible that a cell competition mechanism might lead to elimination of unfit cells (Johnston, 2009).
evidence: This is speculated as another alternative explanation for GB death, supported by a citation to prior work on cell competition.

claim: Unique behaviors of centrosomes in stem cell populations have been reported in multiple stem cell systems.
source: Unique behaviors of centrosomes in stem cell populations have been reported in multiple stem cell systems (Conduit and Raff, 2010; Habib et al., 2013; Januschke et al., 2011, 2013; Rebollo et al., 2007; Rusan and Peifer, 2007; Salzmann et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2009; Yamashita et al., 2003, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies on centrosome behavior in stem cells.

claim: Klp10A's enrichment on the stem cell centrosomes but not on the centrosomes of differentiating SGs suggests the presence of cellular mechanisms unique to stem cell centrosomes.
source: Klp10A's enrichment on the stem cell centrosomes but not on the centrosomes of differentiating SGs suggests the presence of cellular mechanisms unique to stem cell centrosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential localization of Klp10A in GSCs versus SGs.

claim: The stem cell mother centrosome has unique characteristics and modes of regulation.
source: Moreover, klp10A knockdown/mutation led to elongation of the mother centrosome specifically within stem cells; neither the daughter centrosome in GSCs nor any centrosomes in SGs were elongated. This phenotype demonstrates that the stem cell mother centrosome has unique characteristics and modes of regulation and indicates that the GSC mother centrosome has an inherent tendency to elongate, which must be counteracted by Klp10A.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific elongation of mother centrosomes in GSCs upon klp10A depletion.

claim: The mother centrosome in GSCs may have distinct microtubule dynamics, partly because of the necessity for the mother centrosome to be anchored to the hub-GSC interface throughout the cell cycle.
source: The mother centrosome in GSCs may have distinct microtubule dynamics, partly because of the necessity for the mother centrosome to be anchored to the hub-GSC interface throughout the cell cycle (Yamashita et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculated based on prior work showing mother centrosome anchoring and the observed phenotypes.

claim: Loss of function of asterless (asl) results in mother centrosome-specific elongation in Drosophila male GSCs.
source: It is worth noting that the centrosome size itself might not be the cause of asymmetric force generation. It was recently reported that loss of function of asterless (asl), the gene that encodes a core centriolar component, results in mother centrosome-specific elongation in Drosophila male GSCs (Galletta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: asl mutant did not lead to asymmetric spindle formation or daughter cell size.
source: However, asl mutant did not lead to asymmetric spindle formation or daughter cell size, suggesting a unique function for Klp10A.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with the asl mutant phenotype, suggesting Klp10A has a unique function.

claim: Asymmetric spindles, where one half of the spindle is considerably larger than the other, are often observed during normal developmental processes.
source: Asymmetric spindles, where one half of the spindle is considerably larger than the other, are often observed during normal developmental processes.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about developmental biology.

claim: Drosophila neuroblasts divide asymmetrically to produce another neuroblast and a differentiating cell.
source: For example, Drosophila neuroblasts divide asymmetrically to produce another neuroblast and a differentiating cell (either ganglion mother cell in type I neuroblast lineage, or intermediate neural progenitor cell in type II neuroblast lineage) (Doe and Bowerman, 2001; Prehoda, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on neuroblast divisions.

claim: In neuroblast divisions, the self-renewing neuroblast is considerably larger than its differentiating daughter cell.
source: In neuroblast divisions, the self-renewing neuroblast is considerably larger than its differentiating daughter cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuroblast divisions.

claim: The first mitosis of C. elegans zygote is characterized by asymmetric daughter cell sizes.
source: Similarly, the first mitosis of C. elegans zygote is also characterized by asymmetric daughter cell sizes (Rose and Gonczy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on C. elegans development.

claim: Asymmetric spindle morphology contributes to cell size asymmetry together with a myosin-dependent pathway that controls cleavage furrow positioning.
source: Asymmetric spindle morphology contributes to cell size asymmetry together with a myosin-dependent pathway that controls cleavage furrow positioning (Cabernard et al., 2010; Knoblich, 2010; Pacquelet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on mechanisms of asymmetric cell division.

claim: In C. elegans Q lineage neuroblasts, which divide asymmetrically by spindle pulling and asymmetric Myosin localization, the smaller daughter undergoes apoptosis.
source: More interestingly, in C. elegans Q lineage neuroblasts, which divide asymmetrically by spindle pulling and asymmetric Myosin localization, the smaller daughter undergoes apoptosis reminiscent of GBs in klp10ARNAi testes (Ou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on C. elegans Q lineage neuroblasts.

claim: Death of daughter cells that are born too small might be utilized in the context of normal development.
source: This implies that death of daughter cells that are born too small might be utilized in the context of normal development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation in C. elegans Q lineage neuroblasts and the phenotype in klp10ARNAi GSCs.

claim: Multiple aspects of ACDs (e.g. asymmetric segregation of fate determinants, spindle orientation, daughter cell size asymmetry) are carefully calibrated processes to achieve successful ACD unique to individual systems.
source: Our observations described in this study suggest that multiple aspects of ACDs (e.g. asymmetric segregation of fate determinants, spindle orientation, daughter cell size asymmetry) are carefully calibrated processes to achieve successful ACD unique to individual systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that loss of Klp10A leads to excessive asymmetries that compromise cell viability.

claim: The MT-depolymerizing kinesin, Klp10A, counterbalances the mechanism that generates asymmetric centrosome behavior of mother and daughter centrosomes.
source: In summary, our study illuminates a critical mechanism for ACD, in which the MT-depolymerizing kinesin, Klp10A, counterbalances the mechanism that generates asymmetric centrosome behavior of mother and daughter centrosomes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Asymmetry-generating mechanisms are critical for proper spindle orientation and thus ACD of GSCs.
source: Whereas asymmetry-generating mechanisms are critical for proper spindle orientation and thus ACD of GSCs, the lack of a counteracting force by Klp10A results in excessive asymmetries, leading to frequent death of GBs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of Klp10A leads to excessive asymmetries and GB death.

claim: The lack of a counteracting force by Klp10A results in excessive asymmetries, leading to frequent death of GBs.
source: Whereas asymmetry-generating mechanisms are critical for proper spindle orientation and thus ACD of GSCs, the lack of a counteracting force by Klp10A results in excessive asymmetries, leading to frequent death of GBs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing increased GB death in klp10ARNAi testes.

claim: ACD is achieved by fine-tuned symmetries and asymmetries, failure of which can lead to unsuccessful cell divisions.
source: We propose that ACD is achieved by fine-tuned symmetries and asymmetries, failure of which can lead to unsuccessful cell divisions.
evidence: This is the main model proposed based on all the findings in the study.

claim: In control testes, most cell death was observed at the 16-cell stage of SGs, whereas GBs were rarely observed to die.
source: In control testes, most cell death was observed at the 16-cell stage of SGs, whereas GBs were rarely observed to die (Figure 4D,F) (Yang and Yamashita, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 4D and 4F, and a citation to prior work.

claim: There is a basal level of germ cell death under normal conditions in Drosophila testes.
source: Previously, we have shown that there is a basal level of germ cell death under normal conditions (i.e. with optimal nutrient conditions in young flies) (Yang and Yamashita, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: Germ cell death is characterized by acidification of dying cells that is detectable by Lysotracker.
source: Germ cell death is characterized by acidification of dying cells that is detectable by Lysotracker (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013; Yang and Yamashita, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on methods for detecting cell death.

claim: 78% of elongated centrosomes were near the hub in klp10ARNAi GSCs.
source: We assumed that the elongated centrosome is the mother, based on its location near the hub, where the mother centrosome is located (Yamashita et al., 2007) (Figure 2B; In 78% of cases, the elongated centrosomes were near the hub, n = 222 GSCs with elongated centrosomes).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from microscopy analysis.

claim: Klp10A localizes to the central spindle microtubule bundle.
source: Arrowheads indicate Klp10A localization to the central spindle microtubule bundle.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B and shown in the image.

claim: MT-nanotubes are sensitive to regular fixation conditions.
source: It should be noted that MT-nanotubes are sensitive to regular fixation conditions, and its localization on MT-nanotubes is not obvious in the images shown in panel B.
evidence: This is stated as a technical note about the imaging conditions.
